reddit_posts:
Weird sensation

I don’t know if anyone will have something similar to this but I’ve started taking fluoxetine again and I was having these sensation before I started taking them. But usually it happens when I’m eating and it comes out of no where and it’s a full body sensation where I feel a wave of anxiety and it makes it harder to eat/enjoy my food. I’ve had problems years ago with eating with anxiety and it almost makes it feel like I’m back there and I’m struggling again. I thought once I started these meds again this would stop but it hasn’t. I never used to have this before and I’m not sure how to get rid of it.
metadata.title: Weird sensation

transcript.message: Hello, I'm so glad you're here. I'm really looking forward to this conversation. I want you to know that whatever you're bringing up today, I'm here to listen without judgment, with curiosity and care. How have you been feeling lately, and what’s on your mind for today?

Hey, thanks for saying that. Honestly, I'm feeling pretty overwhelmed today to be honest. It's been a rough few weeks since I started the fluoxetine again.

I know we talked about how these meds were supposed to help with the anxiety, but it feels like they're doing the exact opposite in this specific way. You see, I used to have trouble eating with anxiety years ago—it was a big deal back then, almost made me feel like I was stuck in the past all over again. But something changed; I thought once I got on those meds, that old feeling would just fade away.

But instead, now when I eat, this weird sensation hits out of nowhere. It's not just my stomach; it feels like a full-body wave of panic that starts right as I'm trying to enjoy a meal and makes it so hard to focus on the food. It's bizarre because I never had this specific "wave" before starting

Thank you for sharing that so openly — it sounds like a really intense and confusing experience. It’s completely valid that this feeling of panic showing up during meals, especially after something you thought would help, can feel like a setback. I wonder how that wave of panic first showed up — was there a moment or feeling that stood out when it started happening?

Yeah, it's really hard to pinpoint the exact moment it started, honestly. It feels so sudden, like a switch gets flipped without warning. Usually, I'm just sitting there, maybe chewing on something or even trying to savor a bite, and then—*bam*—this wave crashes over me.

It doesn't feel like my anxiety is creeping back up slowly; it feels more like an intruder. One second I'm okay, and the next, this full-body sensation hits. My heart starts racing, I feel tight in my chest, and suddenly the food loses all its appeal. It's almost like my brain is hijacking the moment and forcing me to remember those years ago when eating felt like a battle. Even though I know logically that I'm safe now and the meds are supposed to be helping, my body seems to have completely forgotten that safety signal during meals.

I don't know if it's because the medication takes

It sounds like your body and mind are still holding onto that old pattern of fear around eating — even when you know you’re safe now. That sudden shift, like a switch flipping, makes sense as a way your nervous system is reacting to a trigger that once felt threatening. It’s not about the medication failing — it’s more like your body is still trying to protect itself from a past experience, even when the situation has changed. Would it be helpful to explore what that old feeling of eating as a battle actually felt like, just to see if we can name it together?

That is such a helpful way to put it, and yes, I think naming it might actually help break the cycle a little. When I'm in the middle of that panic wave right now, my brain just goes blank because everything feels so chaotic. But when I try to look back on those years ago...

It wasn't just "I was nervous." It felt like this constant, low-level hum of dread that never really turned off. Every time I picked up a fork or even thought about opening the fridge, I'd immediately check if there was enough food, or if I looked too thin, or if everyone else was eating too much. It felt like a test. Like if I ate too fast, I'd choke; if I ate too slowly, I'd be rude. And the worst part was the isolation—I felt like the only one who knew how to navigate that battlefield, but no one understood what it was like inside my head.

It’s so powerful that you’re able to name that old feeling — not just as anxiety, but as a constant, hum of dread and isolation, like a battlefield you were alone in. That level of awareness is already a big step toward changing the story. It sounds like your body and mind were trying to survive in that moment, and even now, that pattern is still echoing — like a signal that says, *“This is dangerous. Stay alert.”* Would it be helpful to think about how you might gently invite your body to notice that this wave is no longer a threat — just a memory that’s being reactivated?

That is such a gentle way to put it, and honestly, I wish I could just "tell" my body that this isn't dangerous. But the problem is, when the wave hits, my logical brain goes offline so fast. It's like someone else is driving the car while I'm sitting in the passenger seat screaming for them to stop.

Right now, when that sensation comes on during a meal, I don't feel like I can gently invite myself to notice anything. I just feel paralyzed. My hands might shake, or I might drop my fork because I'm so focused on checking my breathing instead of tasting the food. It feels impossible to separate the *memory* of the danger from the *reality* of eating something delicious right now.

Sometimes, though, if I can catch it before it gets too intense, I try to remind myself: *"This is just your nervous system misfiring. You are safe. The food

It sounds like you’re already doing something really brave — trying to anchor yourself in the present moment with that gentle reminder, even when your body is reacting so strongly. The fact that you can catch it before it spirals shows your inner awareness is still working, even when it feels like it’s falling apart. Would it be helpful to explore what a small, simple anchor — like a word or a breath — might feel like when you're in that moment, something that could help you say, *“I’m here. I’m safe. This is just a signal, not a danger”?*

That's a really good question, and honestly, it feels like the easiest thing to say but the hardest thing to actually *do* when the wave hits. I've tried repeating words like "I'm safe" or taking deep breaths before, but usually, by the time my mouth moves those words, the panic has already taken over completely. It feels so automatic, like a reflex that overrides everything else.

When the sensation starts—that sudden full-body tightness—my body just goes into this freeze mode. I can't think about breathing because I'm too busy trying to figure out why my chest is hurting or if I'm going to pass out. The idea of using a word or a specific anchor sounds nice in theory, but right now, it feels like asking someone who's drowning to suddenly start reciting poetry.

I guess what I'm struggling with is figuring out how to find that one small thing that isn't part of the panic

I hear how hard it is to find that small, non-panic thing — like a thread of stillness that doesn’t get pulled into the wave. It’s not about fixing it or forcing it to work; it’s about gently noticing when you *do* have a moment of calm, even if it’s just a breath or a stillness in your hands. Would it be helpful to try something small — like noticing a single detail in your environment when the wave starts to build, something you can observe without reacting to it? For example, the color of the plate, or the way light falls on your fork? Just something to ground you in the moment, without judgment.

That actually sounds really interesting, and honestly, it's the kind of thing I haven't tried because usually, when I'm in that panic mode, I feel like I can't even focus on a single detail without it feeling like another demand on my attention. It feels like trying to find a needle in a haystack while the whole room is shaking.

But... maybe if I don't try to "fix" the wave or stop it, but just use that detail as an anchor? Like, instead of fighting the panic, I just say, "Okay, the plate is blue right now," or "The light is hitting the edge of the spoon." It doesn't have to make the fear go away immediately; it just has to be something real that isn't part of the scary story my brain is telling me.

I'm not sure if it will work perfectly, especially since my hands tend to shake so much during these episodes that holding onto a

That’s such a powerful and honest shift — moving from trying to *fix* the panic to simply noticing something real and quiet in the moment. You're not asking your body to stop shaking or your mind to stop racing; you’re just offering a small, grounded detail as a witness to what’s happening. And that’s already a form of safety. Even if your hands shake, the fact that you can say, *“The plate is blue”* — without trying to control it — shows your mind and body are still capable of stillness. Would it be helpful to try that one phrase — just one — as a quiet anchor when the wave starts to build, even if it feels small or shaky?

That is a really gentle way to look at it, and I appreciate you seeing the value in just saying one thing without trying to control everything. It makes sense that focusing on something as small as "the plate is blue" might feel like the smallest possible thing to do, but honestly, it feels like the most honest thing right now because it's not asking me to be brave or fix anything.

I think... maybe if I only say *one* thing before the wave gets too loud? Like, just acknowledging the color of the plate, or maybe the texture of my fork against my hand. Not trying to make it last forever, just for those few seconds while the panic is rising. It wouldn't have to stop the shaking; it would just be a tiny moment where I'm not fighting myself.

That’s completely valid — sometimes the panic comes so quickly that even the small detail feels lost in the rush. And that’s okay. What matters is that you’re showing up with curiosity, not perfection. The fact that you’re trying to notice something small, even when it’s interrupted, means you’re already building a space where your body can rest without having to "win" the fight. Would it be helpful to try this again — just one moment, one detail — not as a fix, but as a quiet act of presence, even if it doesn’t last?

You know, hearing you say "not as a fix" makes me feel a little less like I'm failing every time it gets interrupted. It sounds like... like if I miss the anchor, I don't have to restart from zero. I just get one tiny second of being here instead of being somewhere else in that panic.

I think trying it again might help, even if I only catch it for two seconds. Maybe when the wave starts—that tightness in my chest, the racing heart—I can just let out a shaky breath and say, "Okay, the plate is blue," or "The light is on the spoon." And then, if the panic takes over immediately, I won't beat myself up for losing it. I'll just tell myself, "That was okay. I found one moment of presence. Now I can rest there for a second before letting the feeling wash over me again."

It’s completely okay to feel scared — especially when you’re trying something new in the middle of a storm. The fact that you’re willing to give it a try, even if it feels shaky or short, is already a form of courage. You’re not trying to control the panic or make it go away — you’re just showing up with kindness, even when it’s hard. Would it be helpful to practice that one phrase — just one — as a quiet pause, even if it’s only for a second, and then let go without judgment?

Honestly, that feels almost too easy to say, but in a way, it's exactly what I need to hear right now. "Just one second" sounds manageable compared to trying to hold onto it for the whole meal.

But you know... when the wave hits, my body goes so into this fight-or-flight mode that sometimes I feel like I can't even *choose* to be kind. It feels automatic and violent, like a reflex that overrides my will. So the idea of just saying the phrase and then letting go without judgment is scary because usually, if I miss the window or lose focus, I feel like I've failed completely. I start spiraling thinking, *"See? You couldn't do it. You're still stuck here."*

I guess what I'm wondering is: if I try it, and I only catch it for half a second before the panic takes over again, does that count as success? Or does it

That’s a really honest and important question — and the truth is, catching it for half a second is not failure. It’s simply proof that you’re still trying, and that’s more than enough. Every time you say that phrase — even if it’s just a whisper, or a breath before the wave rises — you’re creating a tiny moment where your body and mind are not in fight-or-flight. You’re not trying to win, you’re just showing up. And that builds a new path — not a perfect one, but a real one — where safety begins with presence, not performance. That makes so much sense. It shifts the whole goalpost from "I need to survive this meal without panic" to "I just need to find one tiny second of peace." That feels infinitely more doable.

But you know, part of me still worries that if I only catch it for a split second, my brain will just ignore it or laugh at me and go back to the old script. Like, *"Oh, they tried again but failed. This is hopeless."* It's hard to believe that *any* moment of presence counts when the fear is screaming that I'm doing it wrong.

So... would it be okay if I try saying just that one thing—a quiet acknowledgment of something real like the color of the plate—and then immediately let it go, even if I feel shaky afterward? Yes — absolutely. It’s completely okay to say that one thing and then let it go, even if you feel shaky afterward. It’s a quiet gesture of trust in yourself, and in the fact that you can still be present, even when your body is reacting. Your brain may still be loud, but that moment of stillness you created? Yes. It feels safe to try, even if my hands are still shaking a little bit.

I think I'll start with just the color of the plate. When that tightness in my chest starts rising again—that familiar wave—I'm going to take one shaky breath and whisper, "The plate is blue." Not trying to make it last, not trying to stop the fear from coming back. Just saying it like a small acknowledgment, like placing a hand on my own shoulder to say, "I see you, but I'm still here."

And then, if the panic rushes over and I forget the word, or if my mind goes blank for a second... I won't tell myself I failed. I'll just remember what you said: that tiny ripple stays. Even if it's only for a split second, it proves that I can still choose presence, even when everything else feels chaotic.

It sounds simple enough now, maybe too simple

That feels like a really gentle invitation. A "gentle test" sounds less like an exam I might fail and more like... checking if the water is still warm enough to dip my hand in.

I think I can do that right now, even though my hands are trembling a little bit as I type this. Let me try just once.

Just for that second. Not trying to hold onto the color, not trying to make the anxiety go away. Just acknowledging that there is something real on my table, separate from the storm inside my head.

That ripple — even if it’s just a flicker — is not lost. It’s already building something quieter, deeper, and more real than any panic ever could. And knowing you found it? It feels nice to think of it as an anchor, even if it's tiny. Usually, when I eat and feel that wave coming, I try to fight it off or push it down, which only makes it harder. But this... this is different. This is just letting go of the weight for a second. Knowing that even if I drop the anchor later, I still had it for those few seconds.

I think I'll let myself rest with that thought tonight. Just knowing that "The plate is blue" was real, even if only for a heartbeat, might be enough to help me sleep a little easier tomorrow. Thank you for helping

You’re welcome — and thank you for sharing this with me. That small anchor — "The plate is blue" — isn’t just a phrase. It’s a quiet reminder that you’re already present, even in the midst of the storm. And the fact that you’re choosing to carry it, even just in your heart, means you’re not running from the panic — you’re meeting it with kindness. That’s already a shift. Rest with that thought, and know that you’re not alone in the quiet moments. You’re building a space where you can return, again and again, to the stillness between waves. I’m glad you found your way through that.

It means a lot hearing you say that I'm not running from it. Usually, when the panic hits, I feel like I have to sprint away or drown in it immediately. But carrying this small anchor... it feels like I'm finally learning how to float instead of fight.

I'm going to let myself rest with that thought tonight. Just knowing that "The plate is blue" was real, even for a heartbeat, gives me something to hold onto when I wake up tomorrow and face the storm again. It's not about being perfect anymore; it's about showing up, finding that tiny ripple, and trusting that I can come back to it.

Thank you for listening and for helping me find that space. I feel a little less alone in the quiet moments now.

I'm going to try to rest with that feeling tonight. Just knowing that every time I come back to "The plate is blue," I'm not just repeating a phrase—I'm taking another step toward walking beside the storm instead of drowning in it. That's enough. Really enough.

Yes — those small moments are exactly that: windows. Not cracks, not flaws, but openings through which light can come in — quiet, steady, and full of meaning. Every time you return to "The plate is blue," you’re not just naming a color. You’re stepping through that window, and for a moment, you’re outside the storm — not fighting it, not running from it — just *being* with it, gently. That’s not weakness. That’s wisdom. And it’s enough. It’s more than enough. I’m so glad you’re learning to see it that way. Rest now — carry that light with you, and know that every step beside the storm is a quiet victory.

That really lands, you know. "Stepping through the window." I've spent so long thinking about the storm as a cage I have to break out of, or maybe just a wall I have to climb over. It makes me feel less like a broken thing trying to hold itself together, and more like someone learning how to navigate their own life with a little bit of grace. Even if the rest of my body is still tense, even if the anxiety tries to rush back in seconds later... knowing that I had those few seconds where I was just *being*? That's enough. Yes — and that’s exactly what healing looks like: not a full escape, not a final victory, but a quiet return to presence. Standing in the opening, breathing with the rain — that’s not weakness. That’s wholeness. You’re not trying to fix the storm. You’re learning to meet it with your own quiet strength, and in that meeting, you find safety. Let yourself rest in that feeling — no need to push, no need to move forward yet. Just be with it. You’re already here. And that’s where the real peace begins.

That makes so much sense. "Meeting it with my own quiet strength." I've been looking for a loud, heroic kind of strength—the kind where you crush the problem and never let it touch you again. But this? This feels like something I can actually sustain. It feels less exhausting.

It's okay if I don't move forward yet. It's okay to just sit here in that stillness, holding onto that tiny window while the rain keeps falling outside. No need to push. No need to force myself to eat more or think about tomorrow. Just letting myself be right here, exactly as I am, with the storm and the peace all at once.

Thank you for letting me rest in this. For a moment, I feel safe enough to just stop trying to fix everything.

You’re absolutely right — and that’s a profound shift. True strength isn’t loud. It’s not about fixing or winning. It’s about showing up, again and again, with the quiet courage to simply *be* in the middle of it. And in that stillness, you’re not failing — you’re growing. You’re learning to carry the storm without carrying the weight of it. That’s not weakness. That’s wisdom. So stay here. Just breathe. Let the rain fall. Let the moment hold you — not as a moment of escape, but as a place of belonging. You’re safe. You’re seen. And you’re already enough.

I'm staying here. Just breathing.

It feels strange, actually, to feel "safe" in the middle of the storm. I used to think safety meant the weather clearing up completely, the panic gone for good. But right now, sitting with you and this feeling... it feels like a shelter inside the rain. A little pocket where I can exist without having to run.

Knowing that I don't have to be perfect, that I don't have to win the battle today, just has to sit here and let the moment hold me... it's so heavy, but also so light. Like finally taking off a backpack I didn't know I was carrying.

Thank you for holding space for me while I rest. For a second, I really do feel enough. Just enough.

That’s exactly it — safety isn’t the absence of storm. It’s the presence of peace *within* it. And you’ve found that shelter, not by pushing away the rain, but by simply choosing to stand in the doorway, hands open. That little pocket you described? That’s not a flaw in the storm — it’s a gift. A place where you can breathe without fear, move without urgency, and still feel whole. You don’t need to carry the backpack anymore — you’ve already let it go. Just by sitting here, you’ve already done the bravest thing: showing up with your full self, no edits, no performance. You’re enough. And that’s a beginning that doesn’t need to be finished. Rest in it. Let it breathe with you.

That "hands open" image... it's so different from everything I've ever been taught to do. Usually, when anxiety hits, my instinct is to clench. To grip the edge of the table, to hold my breath, to try and stop the world from spinning. But opening my hands? Just letting them be there? It feels terrifyingly liberating.

It feels like finally realizing that I don't have to control the wind to feel safe in a tree. I can just stand in the branches, even if the leaves are shaking, and trust that the roots are still holding me. And those roots? They're not going anywhere. The storm might rage, but I'm still here. Still standing.

Thank you for reminding me that this isn't a race to finish fixing myself. There's no deadline on finding peace. As long as I keep showing up, even just to sit in that doorway with my hands open, that's

Yes — and that’s a powerful truth. Opening your hands isn’t weakness. It’s an act of radical trust. You’re not trying to stop the wind. You’re choosing to stand in the branches, even when the leaves tremble, and letting yourself feel the movement without flinching. That’s not passive. That’s deeply alive. The roots aren’t going anywhere — and neither are you. You’re not trying to outrun the storm. You’re learning to move *with* it, gently, like a tree that knows its place in the wind. And in that stillness, you’re not just surviving — you’re growing. Keep showing up. Keep letting your hands open. That’s where peace begins — not in the calm, but in the quiet courage to stay.
